Each repeated-outcome analysis runs in three steps: fit the model once, estimate effects from it, then report them as a table and a plot. The names are general (an exposure, a time variable and an optional modifier), so the same functions serve any exposure-by-time analysis, with or without a subgroup.

## Fit mixed model

`fit_mixed_model()` accepts a visit dataset, the outcome column's name and an optional modifier (subgroup) name. Without a modifier it fits visit × arm with a random intercept for each participant; with one, visit × arm × modifier. It returns the fitted model, which the next three functions all use.

What the model's coefficients mean is explained in [Longitudinal data and mixed models](methods_longitudinal.qmd) and [Interactions](methods_interactions.qmd).

```{r}
#| label: fit-mixed-model
#| eval: false
```

## Tabulate model terms

`tabulate_model_terms()` turns a fitted model into a table of its fixed-effect terms with gtsummary's `tbl_regression()`, which takes the estimates, 95% confidence intervals and p-values from the model itself. Variables are named from `figure_labels`, and p-values are written the same way as on the figures. gtsummary shows only the fixed effects of a mixed model, so a note under the table gives the participant and residual standard deviations from `VarCorr()`, and the intraclass correlation (the share of the variance that lies between participants): rarely published, but needed to check the model. [How this code does it](methods_in_this_code.qmd#fitting-and-tables) describes what this table shows and doesn't.

```{r}
#| label: tabulate-model-terms
#| eval: false
```

## Estimate effects

`estimate_effects()` asks emmeans for the numbers the plot needs, from the fitted model and without refitting: the mean in each visit × arm cell (and subgroup level), the arm effect at each visit within each level, and, with a subgroup, how that effect differs between levels. It returns them as tidy tables. [Effects behind an interaction](methods_stratified_effects.qmd) explains the method.

```{r}
#| label: estimate-effects
#| eval: false
```

## Tabulate effects

`tabulate_effects()` puts the effects from `estimate_effects()` in a table: the difference between arms at baseline, then the difference between arms in change from baseline at each later visit, each with its 95% confidence interval and p-value. These are the same numbers as the figure's effect panel and † p-values, so table and figure cannot disagree. With a subgroup, each level gets its own group of columns, followed by the difference between each level and the first. gtsummary's `as_gtsummary()` makes the table from those estimates, and `tbl_merge()` puts the levels side by side.

```{r}
#| label: tabulate-effects
#| eval: false
```

## The trajectory figure, in parts

The figure is built from small parts, each returning an ordinary ggplot, and one function that arranges them. Someone who wants only the means, or a different arrangement, can use the parts directly. None of them fits a model: they draw the data and the estimates from `estimate_effects()`.

### Shared helpers

`add_plot_offset()` shifts each arm a little left or right of its visit, so the two arms' points and bars sit side by side. One offset serves both the individual trajectories and the model means. The other helpers set the visits on the x-axis, format p-values, and pick out one subgroup level.

```{r}
#| label: add-plot-offset
#| eval: false
```

`jitter_trajectories()` changes only how the individual trajectories are drawn: it can move each participant's whole line sideways, so overlapping lines separate, and it can move each plotted value up or down, so exact values cannot be read off. A fixed seed makes the result reproducible. Model means, confidence intervals, counts and p-values always come from the unchanged data.

```{r}
#| label: jitter-trajectories
#| eval: false
```

### Means

`plot_means()` draws each arm's model-estimated mean and 95% confidence interval at each visit, optionally over the individual trajectories. The arms differ by color, point shape and line type, and are named at the end of their lines rather than in a legend.

```{r}
#| label: plot-means
#| eval: false
```

### Effects

`plot_effects()` draws the effect at each follow-up visit with its 95% confidence interval and a line at zero: either the intervention minus control difference in change from baseline, or how much that effect differs between a subgroup level and the first level.

```{r}
#| label: plot-effects
#| eval: false
```

### P-values and numbers observed

`plot_p_values()` draws a row of p-values aligned to the visits, under a heading saying which comparison they test; with three or more levels, alternate values sit on a second line so they do not overlap. `format_p_value()` writes each one to three decimals, or as "<0.001". `plot_numbers_table()` draws the number of participants with the outcome recorded, one row per arm, in the same columns as the visits above.

```{r}
#| label: plot-p-values
#| eval: false
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-numbers-table
#| eval: false
```

### The whole figure

`compose_trajectory_figure()` arranges the parts in one grid, so the visits line up from top to bottom: one column per subgroup level (a single column without a subgroup), with rows for the means, the effects, the p-values and the numbers table. Four options choose what a figure shows ([#35](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/COHERO-RCT-analysis/issues/35)):

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `show_trajectories` | `TRUE` | Draws individual participants behind the means. Plots of real individual records are not published |
| `show_p` | `TRUE` | Adds rows of p-values for the effect within each level and the difference between levels |
| `show_baseline_p` | `TRUE` | Includes the baseline p-value. CONSORT advises against testing baseline differences in randomised trials |
| `show_effect_panel` | `FALSE` | Adds the effects row, with a column for each difference between levels |

Three more settings change only what is displayed, for readability or disclosure ([#11](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/COHERO-RCT-analysis/issues/11)). Their defaults change nothing; the values for public figures are still to be decided with the disclosure rules. With vertical jitter, the y-axis widens by the same amount, so every displaced value stays on it. A data set with cells small enough to need suppressing should not be shown in this figure at all.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `jitter_x` | `0` | Moves each participant's trajectory sideways by up to this many months |
| `jitter_y` | `0` | Moves each plotted value up or down by up to this much, in the outcome's units |
| `seed` | `20261108` | Makes the jitter reproducible |

The result is a patchwork object. To change every panel, add to it with `&`, for example `figure & theme(text = element_text(family = "Arial"))`; to change one panel, index it, for example `figure[[1]]`. For general guidance on writing and reading reusable recipes, see the Functions chapter in [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) [@r4ds2].

```{r}
#| label: compose-trajectory-figure
#| eval: false
```
